title: INTEGRATED HYDROGEOTECHNICAL FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE MITIGATION OF SEAWATER INTRUSION USING SOIL CEMENT BARRIERS

INTEGRATED HYDROGEOTECHNICAL FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE MITIGATION OF SEAWATER INTRUSION USING SOIL CEMENT BARRIERS

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Nurnawaty, Abd Rakhim Nanda, Titik Khawa Abd Rahman, Muhammad Faisal
Print ISSN : 2523-5664
Online ISSN : 2523-5672

ABSTRACT

Seawater intrusion is a critical hydrogeotechnical issue affecting the sustainability of coastal aquifers, driven by groundwater over-extraction, land subsidence, and sea-level rise. Unlike previous seawater intrusion mitigation studies that mainly examined hydraulic barriers, cut-off walls, or vulnerability mapping as separate approaches, this study develops an integrated hydrogeotechnical framework that combines laboratory flume validation, MODFLOW–SEAWAT variable-density modelling, response surface optimisation, dimensional scaling, and low-carbon material assessment for soil-cement subsurface barriers. This study presents an integrated experimental numerical framework for assessing the hydraulic performance and sustainability of soil cement subsurface barriers for seawater intrusion mitigation. Laboratory flume experiments demonstrated that intrusion length (L_{x}) decreases nonlinearly with increasing embedment ratio \frac{D}{H}, achieving a maximum reduction of 46% at \frac{D}{H} ≈ 0.4. A SEAWAT-based variable-density model was calibrated and validated with high accuracy (R² = 0.98, RMSE = 0.015 m, NSE = 0.98), accurately reproducing the saline wedge interface. Parametric simulations involving 50 scenarios indicated that reduction efficiency (Pmean) is mainly influenced by barrier depth and hydraulic head difference (ΔH). Response Surface Methodology (RSM) identified optimal depth–thickness combinations through a quadratic interaction model, while dimensional scaling indicated that field-equivalent configurations could achieve more than 50% intrusion reduction under comparable dimensionless conditions. Dimensional scaling verified that laboratory relationships remain valid for \frac{D}{H}\ >0.4 and \frac{B}{L} ≈ 0.006–0.008, supporting design-oriented field-scale interpretation under comparable dimensionless conditions. A sustainability assessment revealed that substituting 30–40% of Portland cement with geopolymer or Microbial-Induced Carbonate Precipitation (MICP) binders reduced embodied CO₂ emissions by up to 45%, while maintaining comparable hydraulic and structural performance.
